authored.description_md: Proves that algebra sections and the source direct-sum definition of segregation agree for nonunital extensions.
authored.proof_md: For a complementary subalgebra, restrict the quotient map to it. The restriction is injective because the intersection with the kernel is zero and surjective because the two subspaces sum to the extension algebra. Its linear inverse is multiplicative since the original map is multiplicative and its restriction is injective. Thus it gives an algebra section. Conversely, a section has a subalgebra as its range. Every element b decomposes as b-s(σ(b)) plus s(σ(b)), and the intersection with the kernel is zero. The restriction is the required algebra isomorphism.
authored.statement_md: [Editorial] Let $\sigma:\mathfrak{B}\to\mathfrak{A}$ be a surjective homomorphism of associative, possibly nonunital algebras over $\Phi$. The extension is segregated in Hochschild's direct-sum sense if and only if there is a $\Phi$-linear multiplicative section $s:\mathfrak{A}\to\mathfrak{B}$ with $\sigma\circ s=\mathrm{id}_{\mathfrak{A}}$. No square-zero condition on the kernel is needed for this equivalence.

authored.proof_md:
The tensor square of the finite-dimensional algebra has finite dimension, hence the cocycle image is finite-dimensional. Adjoin its left-action image, right-action image and mixed-action image. Associativity of the two actions and their commutation show that these four finite-dimensional spaces have a stable sum. Restrict the cocycle to that sum, apply the finite-dimensional singular extension hypothesis, and include its primitive into the original coefficient space. This supplies an explicit finite-support step for the source theorem.

authored.description_md: Proves the scalar-extension construction agrees with Mathlib tensor multiplication, including its full coordinate product formula.
authored.notes_md:
The `mathlib-bypass-proof` warning matches the type constructor TensorProduct,
which is the explicit comparison target of this bridge and an approved linear
algebra foundation. The proof constructs the coefficient equivalence and proves
its multiplication and structure-constant formulas from the source basis.
It does not import a Mathlib separability criterion or replace a source lemma.
Both the source dependency and its Mathlib correspondence remain recorded;
the warning remains visible for this intentional bridge use.
authored.proof_md:
Extend the selected basis to the tensor product and use its coordinate
isomorphism. Each elementary coefficient tuple maps to the corresponding
elementary tensor. Tensor multiplication sends
$(1\otimes a_i)(1\otimes a_j)$ to $1\otimes(a_i a_j)$, whose coordinates are
the embedded original structure constants. Bilinearity and the finite basis
expansions give the formula for arbitrary tuples. Thus this is an equivalence
of the actual source multiplication, not only of the underlying vector spaces.
[uses `Hochschild1945.Def_separable`]
authored.statement_md:
[Editorial bridge] For a selected basis $a_1,\ldots,a_n$, the source coefficient
space is linearly equivalent to $\Gamma\otimes_\Phi\mathfrak A$. The equivalence
sends a tuple $(\gamma_i)$ to $\sum_i\gamma_i(1\otimes a_i)$ and preserves
multiplication. Its multiplication has the original structure constants:
$$(xy)_k=\sum_i\sum_j x_i y_j\,\iota(c_{ijk}),\qquad
  a_i a_j=\sum_k c_{ijk}a_k.$$
No unit in the source algebra is assumed.

authored.description_md: Isolates the classical radical facts used to reduce the kernel of an extension to a nilpotent ideal.
authored.notes_md:
This boundary records nilpotence of the radical, semisimplicity of its quotient, and the zero intersection of a semisimple ideal with the ambient radical, explicitly used in the next paragraph on p. 64. The subsequent homomorphism and kernel calculations are proved in Proposition 6.1 and are not imported conclusions.

Source evidence:

Let $\{\mathfrak{B},\sigma\}$ be any extension of $\mathfrak{A}$, let $\mathfrak{K}$ denote the kernel of the homomorphism $\sigma$, and let $\mathfrak{R}$ denote the radical of $\mathfrak{B}$. Consider $\mathfrak{B}/\mathfrak{R}$: clearly, $(\mathfrak{K}+\mathfrak{R})/\mathfrak{R}$ is an ideal of $\mathfrak{B}/\mathfrak{R}$ (for $\mathfrak{K}$ is an ideal of $\mathfrak{B}$). Since $\mathfrak{B}/\mathfrak{R}$ is semi-simple (we need not consider the case where $\mathfrak{B}$, and hence also $\mathfrak{K}$, is nilpotent), so is $(\mathfrak{K}+\mathfrak{R})/\mathfrak{R}$. Further, $(\mathfrak{K}+\mathfrak{R})/\mathfrak{R}$ is isomorphic with $\mathfrak{K}/\mathfrak{N}$, where $\mathfrak{N}=\mathfrak{K}\cap\mathfrak{R}$. Obviously, $\mathfrak{N}$ is a nilpotent ideal of $\mathfrak{B}$, $\mathfrak{K}/\mathfrak{N}$ is a semi-simple ideal of $\mathfrak{B}/\mathfrak{N}$, and we have the isomorphisms $\mathfrak{A}\cong\mathfrak{B}/\mathfrak{K}\cong(\mathfrak{B}/\mathfrak{N})/(\mathfrak{K}/\mathfrak{N})$.

authored.notes_md:
The source calls this fact well known. It is separate from the following source proof that vanishing first cohomology provides the complement.
A left action is an actual nonunital algebra representation on Module.End. The criterion is the invariant-complement condition printed in the source, for arbitrary coefficient spaces P. No finite-dimensionality or unital-action condition is imposed on P.

authored.statement_md:
As is well known, a necessary and sufficient condition for an algebra to be
semi-simple is that every representation be completely decomposable into
irreducible parts. This in turn is equivalent to the following condition: If
$\mathfrak{P}$ is any left $\mathfrak{A}$-module, $\mathfrak{Q}$ an $\mathfrak{A}$-invariant subspace of $\mathfrak{P}$,
then there exists a (complementary) $\mathfrak{A}$-invariant subspace $\mathfrak{R}$ such that
$\mathfrak{P}$ is the direct sum of $\mathfrak{Q}$ and $\mathfrak{R}$.

authored.proof_md:
Finally, let $f'$ be another $(2,\mathfrak{P})$-cocycle of $\mathfrak{A}$ which is cohomologous to $f$. Then there exists a linear mapping $\tau$ of $\mathfrak{A}$ into $\mathfrak{P}$ such that $f-f'=\delta\tau$, i.e.
\[
f\{a_1,a_2\}=f'\{a_1,a_2\}+a_1\cdot\tau\{a_2\}-\tau\{a_1a_2\}+\tau\{a_1\}\cdot a_2.
\]
Consider the mapping $(a,u)\to I\{(a,u)\}=(a,u+\tau\{a\})$ of $\mathfrak{B}_f$ onto $\mathfrak{B}_{f'}$. We have:

\[
\begin{aligned}
I\{(a_1,u_1)(a_2,u_2)\}
&=(a_1a_2,a_1\cdot u_2+u_1\cdot a_2+f\{a_1,a_2\}+\tau\{a_1a_2\})\\
&=(a_1a_2,a_1\cdot u_2+u_1\cdot a_2+a_1\cdot\tau\{a_2\}+\tau\{a_1\}\cdot a_2+f'\{a_1,a_2\})\\
&=(a_1,u_1+\tau\{a_1\})(a_2,u_2+\tau\{a_2\})=I\{(a_1,u_1)\}I\{(a_2,u_2)\},
\end{aligned}
\]
i.e. $I$ is an isomorphism of $\mathfrak{B}_f$ onto $\mathfrak{B}_{f'}$. Moreover,
\[
\sigma'\{I\{(a,u)\}\}=\sigma'\{(a,u+\tau\{a\})\}=a=\sigma\{(a,u)\}.
\]
Hence the extensions $\{\mathfrak{B}_f,\sigma\}$ and $\{\mathfrak{B}_{f'},\sigma'\}$ are isomorphic. We state the foregoing results in the following proposition:

authored.statement_md: Conversely, suppose that we are given a two-sided $\mathfrak{A}$-module $\mathfrak{P}$ and a $(2,\mathfrak{P})$-cocycle $f$ of $\mathfrak{A}$. Let $\mathfrak{B}$ be the direct sum of the linear space underlying $\mathfrak{A}$ and the linear space $\mathfrak{P}$. Let $(a_1,u_1)$, $(a_2,u_2)$ ($a_i\in\mathfrak{A}$, $u_i\in\mathfrak{P}$) be any two elements of $\mathfrak{B}$. We define their product by the equation $(a_1,u_1)(a_2,u_2)=(a_1a_2,a_1\cdot u_2+u_1\cdot a_2+f\{a_1,a_2\})$. Using the fact that $f$ is a cocycle we verify easily that this multiplication is associative. Hence $\mathfrak{B}$ has been given the structure of an algebra, $\mathfrak{B}_f$, say. The mapping $(a,u)\to\sigma\{(a,u)\}=a$ is obviously a homomorphism of $\mathfrak{B}_f$ onto $\mathfrak{A}$. The kernel of $\sigma$ is the ideal $\mathfrak{K}=(0,\mathfrak{P})$ of $\mathfrak{B}_f$ and, clearly, $\mathfrak{K}^2=\{0\}$. Thus $\{\mathfrak{B}_f,\sigma\}$ is a singular extension of $\mathfrak{A}$. Moreover, if $\rho$ is the mapping $a\to(a,0)$ of $\mathfrak{A}$ into $\mathfrak{B}_f$, $\rho$ satisfies condition (1) and the $(2,\mathfrak{K})$-cocycle $f_\rho$ derived from the extension $\{\mathfrak{B}_f,\sigma\}$ and $\rho$ is (to within a trivial isomorphism) identical with $f$. It is obvious that if $f$ and $f^*$ are corresponding cocycles over operator-isomorphic $\mathfrak{A}$-modules the corresponding extensions of $\mathfrak{A}$ are isomorphic.

authored.description_md: Associates a two-cocycle to a linear section and proves that the resulting cohomology class depends only on the extension.
authored.notes_md:
The `mathlib-bypass-proof` warning matches NonUnitalAlgHom because the extension
projection σ is an actual nonunital algebra homomorphism. This type is also
listed as a correspondence target of the source two-sided-module definition;
its occurrence here does not replace that definition or invoke a counterpart
cohomology theorem. The proof uses the source kernelModule, constructs
ρ(a)ρ(b)−ρ(ab) by TensorProduct.lift, and expands the source coboundary to prove

proof dependencies remain present and verified.
authored.proof_md:
If $\rho'$ is a second linear mapping of $\mathfrak{A}$ into $\mathfrak{B}$ satisfying (1), we have:
\[
\begin{aligned}
f_\rho\{a_1,a_2\}-f_{\rho'}\{a_1,a_2\}
&=\rho\{a_1\}[\rho\{a_2\}-\rho'\{a_2\}]\\
&\quad-[\rho\{a_1a_2\}-\rho'\{a_1a_2\}]+[\rho\{a_1\}-\rho'\{a_1\}]\rho'\{a_2\}\\
&=a_1\cdot[\rho\{a_2\}-\rho'\{a_2\}]-[\rho\{a_1a_2\}-\rho'\{a_1a_2\}]\\
&\quad+[\rho\{a_1\}-\rho'\{a_1\}]\cdot a_2,
\end{aligned}
\]
i.e. $f_\rho-f_{\rho'}=\delta(\rho-\rho')$. Hence the cohomology class $\bar f$ of $f_\rho$ is uniquely determined by the extension $\{\mathfrak{B},\sigma\}$.

Now let $\{\mathfrak{B}^*,\sigma^*\}$ be a singular extension of $\mathfrak{A}$ which is isomorphic (by the isomorphism $I$) with $\{\mathfrak{B},\sigma\}$. Then $I\rho$ is clearly a linear mapping of $\mathfrak{A}$ into $\mathfrak{B}^*$ which satisfies (1). Hence $f_{I\rho}$ is a $(2,\mathfrak{K}^*)$-cocycle of $\mathfrak{A}$ which lies in the cohomology class determined by the extension $\{\mathfrak{B}^*,\sigma^*\}$. Since $f_{I\rho}=If_\rho$, the cohomology class determined by the extension $\{\mathfrak{B}^*,\sigma^*\}$ is the isomorphic image by $I$ of the cohomology class determined by $\{\mathfrak{B},\sigma\}$.

authored.description_md: Constructs the kernel bimodule of a singular extension and shows that it is independent of the chosen linear section.
authored.proof_md:
Since the difference of any two mappings $\rho$ satisfying (1) is a mapping of $\mathfrak{A}$ into $\mathfrak{K}$ and since $\mathfrak{K}^2=\{0\}$ it is clear that $k\cdot a$ and $a\cdot k$ are independent of the particular mapping $\rho$ we have selected. Thus the two-sided $\mathfrak{A}$-module $\mathfrak{K}$ is uniquely determined by the extension $\{\mathfrak{B},\sigma\}$. Furthermore, if $\{\mathfrak{B}^*,\sigma^*\}$ is an isomorphic extension, we have:
\[
\sigma^*\{\rho^*\{a\}\}=a=\sigma\{\rho\{a\}\}=\sigma^*I\{\rho\{a\}\},\quad\hbox{i.e. }\rho^*\{a\}\equiv I\{\rho\{a\}\}\bmod\mathfrak{K}^*.
\]
Hence,
\[
a\cdot I\{k\}=\rho^*\{a\}I\{k\}=I\{\rho\{a\}\}I\{k\}=I\{a\cdot k\},
\]

and, similarly,
\[
I\{k\}\cdot a=I\{k\cdot a\}.
\]
This means that $I$ is an operator isomorphism between the two-sided $\mathfrak{A}$-modules $\mathfrak{K}$ and $\mathfrak{K}^*$, and we have shown that isomorphic extensions lead to operator-isomorphic $\mathfrak{A}$-modules.

authored.notes_md:
The source uses “isomorphism” in the historical sense of an injective homomorphism onto its image: the preceding argument proves a zero-kernel criterion, not surjectivity. Accordingly the Lean statement uses Function.Injective. The quotient is represented by a genuinely surjective algebra homomorphism π:A→C. The original proof paragraph is preserved.

The local proof is complete and contains no `sorry`. In the forward direction, subtract a primitive for the restriction to obtain a cocycle vanishing on the ideal. The cocycle identity puts its values in the two-sided annihilator, so it descends to a quotient cocycle. Theorem 4.1 supplies one primitive there, which combines with the first primitive. No choice-independent assignment of quotient cohomology classes is asserted. In the reverse direction, inflate any quotient cocycle to a quotient module regarded as an A-module. Its restriction is zero, so injectivity gives a primitive; surjectivity of π proves the same primitive works on C. Coefficient modules remain arbitrary.

Theorem 4.1 now has a complete local proof relative to its explicit classical cited boundaries. The false Theorem 5.1 is never invoked. Its source-only proof dependency remains declared and explained by the proof-route deviation (`deps_diff.declared_not_verified.proof`). Genuine kernel/annihilator constructions are isolated in Aux_Thm_5_1_quotient_module, which has no logical dependency on the false claim. The counterexample to Theorem 5.1 does not refute this corollary's universal quantification over every coefficient module.

The opening word is on printed page 60; the definition continues on page 61.
`BasisExtension n Γ` is the actual finite coefficient space `Fin n → Γ`.
Its additive and scalar operations are the ordinary coordinate operations; its
multiplication is transferred through the extended-basis coordinate map. The

authored.statement_md:
We recall that an algebra $\mathfrak{A}$ over the field $\Phi$ is said to be separable if
$\mathfrak{A}_\Gamma$ is semi-simple for every extension field $\Gamma$ of $\Phi$. Here,
$\mathfrak{A}_\Gamma$ denotes the algebra over $\Gamma$ which consists of all linear
combinations $\sum_{i=1}^n\gamma_i a_i$, where $\gamma_i\in\Gamma$ and where
$a_1$, $\cdots$, $a_n$ constitute a basis of $\mathfrak{A}$ over $\Phi$, multiplication
being derived from the multiplication of the $a_i$ in $\mathfrak{A}$ over
$\Phi$.\textsuperscript{7}

[Footnote 7] From here on we shall make use of the classical results in the
theory of separable algebras without giving specific references. The results in
question can be found in any of the standard expositions, such as: Deuring,
``\textit{Algebren}''; Van der Waerden, ``\textit{Moderne Algebra}''; or Jacobson,
loc. cit.
authored.title: Separable algebras

Let $\mathfrak{A}$ be an associative algebra, over an arbitrary field $\Phi$. We consider
linear spaces $\mathfrak{P}$ over $\Phi$ which are at the same time $\mathfrak{A}$-left modules
and $\mathfrak{A}$-right modules\textsuperscript{4}. If $a\in\mathfrak{A}$ we denote the
corresponding $\Phi$-endomorphisms\textsuperscript{5} of $\mathfrak{P}$ by
$u\to a\cdot u$, $u\to u\cdot a$ respectively. In addition to the usual
requirements on these operations for one-sided modules we demand that, if
$a_1$, $a_2\in\mathfrak{A}$ and $u\in\mathfrak{P}$,
$(a_1\cdot u)\cdot a_2=a_1\cdot(u\cdot a_2)$. Then $\mathfrak{P}$ is called a
two-sided $\mathfrak{A}$-module.

authored.proof_md:
We shall do this
by making an induction on the dimension $m$ of $f$: For $m=0$, $f\in\mathfrak{P}$,
and $\delta f\{a\}=a\cdot f-f\cdot a$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\delta\delta f\{a_1,a_2\}
&=a_1\cdot\delta f\{a_2\}-\delta f\{a_1a_2\}+\delta f\{a_1\}\cdot a_2\\
&=a_1\cdot(a_2\cdot f-f\cdot a_2)-(a_1a_2\cdot f-f\cdot a_1a_2)
 +(a_1\cdot f-f\cdot a_1)\cdot a_2\\
&=0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Corresponding to any element $f$ of $(\mathfrak{A}^{(m)}:\mathfrak{P})$, $m\geqq 1$, we define
an element $\bar f\in(\mathfrak{A}^{(m-1)}:(\mathfrak{A}:\mathfrak{P}))$ by the relation
$\bar f\{a_1,\cdots,a_{m-1}\}\{a_m\}=f\{a_1,\cdots,a_m\}$.
(We identify $(\mathfrak{A}^{(0)}:(\mathfrak{A}:\mathfrak{P}))$ with $(\mathfrak{A}:\mathfrak{P})$). Then we can verify
directly from Definition 2.1 that, if $f\in(\mathfrak{A}^{(m)}:\mathfrak{P})$, $m\geqq 1$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\delta f\{a_1,\cdots,a_{m+1}\}
&=(a_1*\bar f\{a_2,\cdots,a_m\})\{a_{m+1}\}\\
&\quad+\sum_{i=1}^{m-1}(-1)^i\bar f\{a_1,\cdots,a_i a_{i+1},\cdots,a_m\}\{a_{m+1}\}\\
&\quad+(-1)^m(\bar f\{a_1,\cdots,a_{m-1}\}*a_m)\{a_{m+1}\}\\
&=\delta\bar f\{a_1,\cdots,a_m\}\{a_{m+1}\},\quad\hbox{whence}\quad
\overline{\delta f}=\delta\bar f.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus, $\overline{\delta\delta f}=\delta\overline{\delta f}=\delta\delta\bar f$.

Since $\dim(\bar f)=\dim(f)-1$, and since $\bar f=0$ only if $f=0$, we can
now apply induction to prove our result.

authored.notes_md:
This independent argument occurs inside the proof of Proposition 6.1 and uses classical facts about the radical and semisimple quotients.

The Lean statement uses the standing finite-dimensional algebra setting; it
does not assert this conclusion for arbitrary infinite-dimensional rings.
The quotient is represented by a surjective nonunital algebra homomorphism
whose kernel is exactly the source radical. The image and inverse image ideals
are constructed from this actual homomorphism. The proof itself contains no
`sorry`; its two separately identified cited nodes retain the external results.
authored.proof_md: For, if $\mathfrak{H}$ is the radical of $\mathfrak{C}$ we have $\mathfrak{S}\cap\mathfrak{H}=\{0\}$; $\mathfrak{C}/\mathfrak{H}$ is semi-simple [uses `Hochschild1945.Cited_radical_structure`] and contains the semi-simple ideal $(\mathfrak{S}+\mathfrak{H})/\mathfrak{H}\cong\mathfrak{S}$. Hence $\mathfrak{C}/\mathfrak{H}$ is the direct sum of $(\mathfrak{S}+\mathfrak{H})/\mathfrak{H}$ and another ideal $\mathfrak{U}$. [uses `Hochschild1945.Cited_semisimple_ideal_structure`] Clearly, there exists an ideal $\mathfrak{T}\ (\supset\mathfrak{H})$ of $\mathfrak{C}$ such that $\mathfrak{U}=\mathfrak{T}/\mathfrak{H}$. Since $\mathfrak{U}\cap(\mathfrak{S}+\mathfrak{H})/\mathfrak{H}=\{0\}$ we have $\mathfrak{T}\cap\mathfrak{S}\subset\mathfrak{H}$, and since $\mathfrak{S}\cap\mathfrak{H}=\{0\}$ this implies that $\mathfrak{T}\cap\mathfrak{S}=\{0\}$. Thus, $\mathfrak{C}$ is the direct sum of $\mathfrak{S}$ and $\mathfrak{T}$.
authored.statement_md: Now, if $\mathfrak{C}$ is any algebra and $\mathfrak{S}$ a semi-simple ideal of $\mathfrak{C}$ then $\mathfrak{C}$ is the direct sum of $\mathfrak{S}$ and another ideal $\mathfrak{T}$.

authored.proof_md:
The linear space $(\mathfrak{A}^{(1)}:\mathfrak{P})$ formed by the $(1,\mathfrak{P})$-cochains of
$\mathfrak{A}$ will play an important part in what follows. We make $(\mathfrak{A}^{(1)}:\mathfrak{P})$
into a two-sided $\mathfrak{A}$-module in a way specially adapted to our purpose: If
$f\in(\mathfrak{A}^{(1)}:\mathfrak{P})$ and $a\in\mathfrak{A}$ we define an element $a*f$ of
$(\mathfrak{A}^{(1)}:\mathfrak{P})$ as follows: $(a*f)\{a'\}=a\cdot f\{a'\}$, for every
$a'\in\mathfrak{A}$. Clearly, this makes $(\mathfrak{A}^{(1)}:\mathfrak{P})$ into an $\mathfrak{A}$-left module.
Furthermore, we define an element $f*a$ of $(\mathfrak{A}^{(1)}:\mathfrak{P})$ by setting
$(f*a)\{a'\}=f\{aa'\}-f\{a\}\cdot a'$, for every $a'\in\mathfrak{A}$. It can be
verified directly that the operation $f\to f*a$ makes $(\mathfrak{A}^{(1)}:\mathfrak{P})$ into
an $\mathfrak{A}$-right module and that $(\mathfrak{A}^{(1)}:\mathfrak{P})$ has in fact become a two-sided
$\mathfrak{A}$-module. We state these facts in the following proposition:
authored.statement_md:
The linear space $(\mathfrak{A}^{(1)}:\mathfrak{P})$ of the $(1,\mathfrak{P})$-cochains of $\mathfrak{A}$ is a
two-sided $\mathfrak{A}$-module with the operations $f\to a*f$ and $f\to f*a$, where
\[
(a*f)\{a'\}=a\cdot f\{a'\}\quad\hbox{and}
\]
\[
(f*a)\{a'\}=f\{aa'\}-f\{a\}\cdot a'.
\]

authored.proof_md:
We shall show first that we can reduce the problem to the case where the kernel $\mathfrak{K}$ of the extension is nilpotent. Specifically, we suppose that $\mathfrak{A}$ is segregated in every extension with nilpotent kernel and prove that then $\mathfrak{A}$ is segregated in every extension.

Let $\{\mathfrak{B},\sigma\}$ be any extension of $\mathfrak{A}$, let $\mathfrak{K}$ denote the kernel of the homomorphism $\sigma$, and let $\mathfrak{R}$ denote the radical of $\mathfrak{B}$. Consider $\mathfrak{B}/\mathfrak{R}$: clearly, $(\mathfrak{K}+\mathfrak{R})/\mathfrak{R}$ is an ideal of $\mathfrak{B}/\mathfrak{R}$ (for $\mathfrak{K}$ is an ideal of $\mathfrak{B}$). Since $\mathfrak{B}/\mathfrak{R}$ is semi-simple (we need not consider the case where $\mathfrak{B}$, and hence also $\mathfrak{K}$, is nilpotent), so is $(\mathfrak{K}+\mathfrak{R})/\mathfrak{R}$. [uses `Hochschild1945.Cited_semisimple_ideal_structure`] Further, $(\mathfrak{K}+\mathfrak{R})/\mathfrak{R}$ is isomorphic with $\mathfrak{K}/\mathfrak{N}$, where $\mathfrak{N}=\mathfrak{K}\cap\mathfrak{R}$. Obviously, $\mathfrak{N}$ is a nilpotent ideal of $\mathfrak{B}$, [uses `Hochschild1945.Cited_radical_structure`] $\mathfrak{K}/\mathfrak{N}$ is a semi-simple ideal of $\mathfrak{B}/\mathfrak{N}$, and we have the isomorphisms $\mathfrak{A}\cong\mathfrak{B}/\mathfrak{K}\cong(\mathfrak{B}/\mathfrak{N})/(\mathfrak{K}/\mathfrak{N})$.

Now, if $\mathfrak{C}$ is any algebra and $\mathfrak{S}$ a semi-simple ideal of $\mathfrak{C}$ then $\mathfrak{C}$ is the direct sum of $\mathfrak{S}$ and another ideal $\mathfrak{T}$. For, if $\mathfrak{H}$ is the radical of $\mathfrak{C}$ we have $\mathfrak{S}\cap\mathfrak{H}=\{0\}$; $\mathfrak{C}/\mathfrak{H}$ is semi-simple and contains the semi-simple ideal $(\mathfrak{S}+\mathfrak{H})/\mathfrak{H}\cong\mathfrak{S}$. Hence $\mathfrak{C}/\mathfrak{H}$ is the direct sum of $(\mathfrak{S}+\mathfrak{H})/\mathfrak{H}$ and another ideal $\mathfrak{U}$. Clearly, there exists an ideal $\mathfrak{T}\ (\supset\mathfrak{H})$ of $\mathfrak{C}$ such that $\mathfrak{U}=\mathfrak{T}/\mathfrak{H}$. Since $\mathfrak{U}\cap(\mathfrak{S}+\mathfrak{H})/\mathfrak{H}=\{0\}$ we have $\mathfrak{T}\cap\mathfrak{S}\subset\mathfrak{H}$, and since $\mathfrak{S}\cap\mathfrak{H}=\{0\}$ this implies that $\mathfrak{T}\cap\mathfrak{S}=\{0\}$. Thus, $\mathfrak{C}$ is the direct sum of $\mathfrak{S}$ and $\mathfrak{T}$. [uses `Hochschild1945.Lem_semisimple_ideal_summand`]

Applying this to the above we conclude that there exists an ideal $\bar{\mathfrak{D}}$ of $\mathfrak{B}/\mathfrak{N}$ such that $\mathfrak{A}\cong\bar{\mathfrak{D}}$. But $\bar{\mathfrak{D}}$ is of the form $\mathfrak{D}/\mathfrak{N}$, where $\mathfrak{D}$ is an ideal of $\mathfrak{B}$, and there is a homomorphism of $\mathfrak{D}$ onto $\mathfrak{A}$ with the nilpotent kernel $\mathfrak{N}$. By hypothesis, there exists a subalgebra $\mathfrak{A}^*$ of $\mathfrak{D}$ such that $\mathfrak{A}^*\cong\mathfrak{A}$ and $\mathfrak{D}$ is the direct sum of $\mathfrak{N}$ and $\mathfrak{A}^*$. Obviously, $\mathfrak{A}^*$ is also a subalgebra of $\mathfrak{B}$, and $\mathfrak{B}$ is the direct sum of $\mathfrak{K}$ and $\mathfrak{A}^*$, i.e. $\mathfrak{A}$ is segregated in $\{\mathfrak{B},\sigma\}$.

It remains to show that if $\mathfrak{A}$ is segregated in every singular extension then $\mathfrak{A}$ is segregated in every extension whose kernel is nilpotent. This we prove by an induction on the dimension of the kernel. If the kernel is of dimension 0, $\mathfrak{B}$ is isomorphic with $\mathfrak{A}$ and there is nothing to prove. Suppose now that the dimension of the nilpotent kernel is $n$, and that our result has already been established for all extensions with a nilpotent kernel of dimension less than $n$. The homomorphism $\sigma$ of $\mathfrak{B}$ onto $\mathfrak{A}$ induces a homomorphism $\bar\sigma$ of $\mathfrak{B}/\mathfrak{K}^2$ onto $\mathfrak{A}$ whose kernel is $\mathfrak{K}/\mathfrak{K}^2$, so that $\{\mathfrak{B}/\mathfrak{K}^2,\bar\sigma\}$ is a singular extension of $\mathfrak{A}$. Hence there exists a subalgebra $\bar{\mathfrak{A}}$ of $\mathfrak{B}/\mathfrak{K}^2$ such that $\bar{\mathfrak{A}}\cong\mathfrak{A}$ and $\mathfrak{B}/\mathfrak{K}^2$ is the direct sum of $\mathfrak{K}/\mathfrak{K}^2$ and $\bar{\mathfrak{A}}$. Let $\mathfrak{C}$ be the subalgebra of $\mathfrak{B}$ such that $\mathfrak{C}/\mathfrak{K}^2=\bar{\mathfrak{A}}$. Then there exists a homomorphism $\sigma$ of $\mathfrak{C}$ onto $\mathfrak{A}$ whose kernel is $\mathfrak{K}^2$. Since $\mathfrak{K}$ is nilpotent, $\dim(\mathfrak{K}^2)<n$, and it follows from our inductive hypothesis that there exists a subalgebra $\mathfrak{A}^*$ of $\mathfrak{C}$ such that $\mathfrak{A}^*\cong\mathfrak{A}$ and $\mathfrak{C}$ is the direct sum of $\mathfrak{K}^2$ and $\mathfrak{A}^*$. Clearly, $\mathfrak{A}^*$ is also a subalgebra of $\mathfrak{B}$ and $\mathfrak{B}$ is the direct sum of $\mathfrak{K}$ and $\mathfrak{A}^*$. This completes the proof of Proposition 6.1.

authored.proof_md:
Let $\{\mathfrak{B},\sigma\}$ be a singular extension of $\mathfrak{A}$ with kernel $\mathfrak{K}$. Let $\rho$ be any linear mapping of $\mathfrak{A}$ into $\mathfrak{B}$ such that
\[
\sigma\{\rho\{a\}\}=a,\quad\hbox{for every } a\in\mathfrak{A},\quad\hbox{or---which is equivalent---}
\]
\begin{equation}\tag{1}
\rho\{\sigma\{b\}\}\equiv b\bmod\mathfrak{K},\quad\hbox{for every }b\in\mathfrak{B}.
\end{equation}

We can make $\mathfrak{K}$ a two-sided $\mathfrak{A}$-module by the definitions $a\cdot k=\rho\{a\}k$, $k\cdot a=k\rho\{a\}$, where $k\in\mathfrak{K}$, $a\in\mathfrak{A}$. Since the difference of any two mappings $\rho$ satisfying (1) is a mapping of $\mathfrak{A}$ into $\mathfrak{K}$ and since $\mathfrak{K}^2=\{0\}$ it is clear that $k\cdot a$ and $a\cdot k$ are independent of the particular mapping $\rho$ we have selected. Thus the two-sided $\mathfrak{A}$-module $\mathfrak{K}$ is uniquely determined by the extension $\{\mathfrak{B},\sigma\}$. Furthermore, if $\{\mathfrak{B}^*,\sigma^*\}$ is an isomorphic extension, we have:
\[
\sigma^*\{\rho^*\{a\}\}=a=\sigma\{\rho\{a\}\}=\sigma^*I\{\rho\{a\}\},\quad\hbox{i.e. }\rho^*\{a\}\equiv I\{\rho\{a\}\}\bmod\mathfrak{K}^*.
\]
Hence,
\[
a\cdot I\{k\}=\rho^*\{a\}I\{k\}=I\{\rho\{a\}\}I\{k\}=I\{a\cdot k\},
\]

and, similarly,
\[
I\{k\}\cdot a=I\{k\cdot a\}.
\]
This means that $I$ is an operator isomorphism between the two-sided $\mathfrak{A}$-modules $\mathfrak{K}$ and $\mathfrak{K}^*$, and we have shown that isomorphic extensions lead to operator-isomorphic $\mathfrak{A}$-modules. [uses `Hochschild1945.Con_extension_module`]

Consider now the mapping $a_1\times a_2\to f_\rho\{a_1,a_2\}=\rho\{a_1\}\rho\{a_2\}-\rho\{a_1a_2\}$ of $\mathfrak{A}\times\mathfrak{A}$ into $\mathfrak{K}$. It is easy to verify that $f_\rho$ is a $(2,\mathfrak{K})$-cocycle of $\mathfrak{A}$.

If $\rho'$ is a second linear mapping of $\mathfrak{A}$ into $\mathfrak{B}$ satisfying (1), we have:
\[
\begin{aligned}
f_\rho\{a_1,a_2\}-f_{\rho'}\{a_1,a_2\}
&=\rho\{a_1\}[\rho\{a_2\}-\rho'\{a_2\}]\\
&\quad-[\rho\{a_1a_2\}-\rho'\{a_1a_2\}]+[\rho\{a_1\}-\rho'\{a_1\}]\rho'\{a_2\}\\
&=a_1\cdot[\rho\{a_2\}-\rho'\{a_2\}]-[\rho\{a_1a_2\}-\rho'\{a_1a_2\}]\\
&\quad+[\rho\{a_1\}-\rho'\{a_1\}]\cdot a_2,
\end{aligned}
\]
i.e. $f_\rho-f_{\rho'}=\delta(\rho-\rho')$. Hence the cohomology class $\bar f$ of $f_\rho$ is uniquely determined by the extension $\{\mathfrak{B},\sigma\}$. [uses `Hochschild1945.Con_extension_cocycle`]

Now let $\{\mathfrak{B}^*,\sigma^*\}$ be a singular extension of $\mathfrak{A}$ which is isomorphic (by the isomorphism $I$) with $\{\mathfrak{B},\sigma\}$. Then $I\rho$ is clearly a linear mapping of $\mathfrak{A}$ into $\mathfrak{B}^*$ which satisfies (1). Hence $f_{I\rho}$ is a $(2,\mathfrak{K}^*)$-cocycle of $\mathfrak{A}$ which lies in the cohomology class determined by the extension $\{\mathfrak{B}^*,\sigma^*\}$. Since $f_{I\rho}=If_\rho$, the cohomology class determined by the extension $\{\mathfrak{B}^*,\sigma^*\}$ is the isomorphic image by $I$ of the cohomology class determined by $\{\mathfrak{B},\sigma\}$.

Conversely, suppose that we are given a two-sided $\mathfrak{A}$-module $\mathfrak{P}$ and a $(2,\mathfrak{P})$-cocycle $f$ of $\mathfrak{A}$. Let $\mathfrak{B}$ be the direct sum of the linear space underlying $\mathfrak{A}$ and the linear space $\mathfrak{P}$. Let $(a_1,u_1)$, $(a_2,u_2)$ ($a_i\in\mathfrak{A}$, $u_i\in\mathfrak{P}$) be any two elements of $\mathfrak{B}$. We define their product by the equation $(a_1,u_1)(a_2,u_2)=(a_1a_2,a_1\cdot u_2+u_1\cdot a_2+f\{a_1,a_2\})$. Using the fact that $f$ is a cocycle we verify easily that this multiplication is associative. Hence $\mathfrak{B}$ has been given the structure of an algebra, $\mathfrak{B}_f$, say. The mapping $(a,u)\to\sigma\{(a,u)\}=a$ is obviously a homomorphism of $\mathfrak{B}_f$ onto $\mathfrak{A}$. The kernel of $\sigma$ is the ideal $\mathfrak{K}=(0,\mathfrak{P})$ of $\mathfrak{B}_f$ and, clearly, $\mathfrak{K}^2=\{0\}$. Thus $\{\mathfrak{B}_f,\sigma\}$ is a singular extension of $\mathfrak{A}$. Moreover, if $\rho$ is the mapping $a\to(a,0)$ of $\mathfrak{A}$ into $\mathfrak{B}_f$, $\rho$ satisfies condition (1) and the $(2,\mathfrak{K})$-cocycle $f_\rho$ derived from the extension $\{\mathfrak{B}_f,\sigma\}$ and $\rho$ is (to within a trivial isomorphism) identical with $f$. It is obvious that if $f$ and $f^*$ are corresponding cocycles over operator-isomorphic $\mathfrak{A}$-modules the corresponding extensions of $\mathfrak{A}$ are isomorphic.

Finally, let $f'$ be another $(2,\mathfrak{P})$-cocycle of $\mathfrak{A}$ which is cohomologous to $f$. Then there exists a linear mapping $\tau$ of $\mathfrak{A}$ into $\mathfrak{P}$ such that $f-f'=\delta\tau$, i.e. [uses `Hochschild1945.Def_2_1`]
\[
f\{a_1,a_2\}=f'\{a_1,a_2\}+a_1\cdot\tau\{a_2\}-\tau\{a_1a_2\}+\tau\{a_1\}\cdot a_2.
\]
Consider the mapping $(a,u)\to I\{(a,u)\}=(a,u+\tau\{a\})$ of $\mathfrak{B}_f$ onto $\mathfrak{B}_{f'}$. We have:

\[
\begin{aligned}
I\{(a_1,u_1)(a_2,u_2)\}
&=(a_1a_2,a_1\cdot u_2+u_1\cdot a_2+f\{a_1,a_2\}+\tau\{a_1a_2\})\\
&=(a_1a_2,a_1\cdot u_2+u_1\cdot a_2+a_1\cdot\tau\{a_2\}+\tau\{a_1\}\cdot a_2+f'\{a_1,a_2\})\\
&=(a_1,u_1+\tau\{a_1\})(a_2,u_2+\tau\{a_2\})=I\{(a_1,u_1)\}I\{(a_2,u_2)\},
\end{aligned}
\]
i.e. $I$ is an isomorphism of $\mathfrak{B}_f$ onto $\mathfrak{B}_{f'}$. Moreover,
\[
\sigma'\{I\{(a,u)\}\}=\sigma'\{(a,u+\tau\{a\})\}=a=\sigma\{(a,u)\}.
\]
Hence the extensions $\{\mathfrak{B}_f,\sigma\}$ and $\{\mathfrak{B}_{f'},\sigma'\}$ are isomorphic. [uses `Hochschild1945.Con_cocycle_extension`] We state the foregoing results in the following proposition:

authored.notes_md:
The proof precedes the theorem on printed pp. 61–63. The principal statement
retains the actual source first-cohomology quotient, the scalar-extension
separability predicate, and arbitrary coefficient modules P. There is no local
`sorry` in this proof. The explicitly cited classical results remain external
boundaries.

The forward implication follows the printed order. It first obtains the source
identity e and replaces f by e·f with an explicit inner correction. The
normalized map remains in the same coefficient carrier P, with the proved
equation e·g(a)=g(a), instead of introducing a new subtype for e·P. This is
exactly the source image condition and imposes no unit action on all of P. Scalar
extension uses the actual tensor spaces Γ⊗A and Γ⊗P and the bilinear extension of
the source actions. The source's chosen-basis coefficient algebra is transported
to this tensor algebra through the proved coordinate equivalence. After the
classical finite splitting extension, the primitive is the displayed finite sum
of selected row and column matrix units. The ground-field descent applies a
K-linear coefficient functional τ:Γ→K with τ(1)=1 to the primitive. This is an
explicit realization of the source's linear-system descent, and it does not
require P to be finite dimensional.

For the converse, the proof constructs the actual projected actions S_a and Q_a
on a chosen complement and on the invariant subspace. The off-diagonal cocycle
has coefficients Hom(S,Q). Its inner primitive corrects the projection, whose
kernel is proved equal to the source graph s↦s−M₀(s). The resulting invariant
complement gives semisimplicity through the explicitly cited representation
criterion.

The classical inseparable simple-component reduction is recorded separately in
Cited_inseparable_simple_component. The component is an actual two-sided ideal,
and an algebra retraction fixes its inclusion. Inflating a cocycle along that
retraction and restricting a primitive along the inclusion are proved directly;
no cohomological conclusion is built into the cited structure theorem.

For the simple algebra, the actual center-field equivalence supplies the scalar
action. Simplicity proves that the image of the field identity acts as the
identity on A; no unital algebra structure is assumed in the principal statement.
The regular representation is expressed in a finite basis over the center.
Applying the derivation of Lemma 4.1 entrywise gives the printed matrix cocycle.
At a center scalar matrix, every inner cocycle is zero whereas this cocycle is
nonzero for some scalar. Lemma 4.1 is used only for the finite-dimensional center,
within its explicitly reviewed finite-extension scope.

The source excerpts and footnotes are retained. The additional direct imports
of the cochain, cocycle and coboundary definitions provide the formal context for
converting the actual quotient's vanishing to innerness. The AlgebraIdeal API in
Def_natural_homomorphism supplies the already declared source ideals used by the
classical component theorem; this is a formalization dependency, not a claim that
the original proof cited the later natural-map construction.
authored.proof_md:
Now, let $\mathfrak{A}$ be a separable algebra over $\Phi$, and let $\mathfrak{P}$ be any
two-sided $\mathfrak{A}$-module. $\mathfrak{A}$ has an identity element: $e$, say. [uses `Hochschild1945.Cited_separable_identity`] For any element
$u\in\mathfrak{P}$ we may write $u=e\cdot u+(1-e)\cdot u$, where 1 stands for the
identity operator on $\mathfrak{P}$. This gives a direct decomposition of $\mathfrak{P}$ into
the $\mathfrak{A}$-invariant linear subspaces $e\cdot\mathfrak{P}$ and $(1-e)\cdot\mathfrak{P}$.
If $f$ is any $(1,\mathfrak{P})$-cocycle of $\mathfrak{A}$ we have
\[
(1-e)\cdot f\{a\}=(1-e)\cdot f\{ea\}=(1-e)\cdot f\{e\}\cdot a.
\]
If we set $u=(1-e)\cdot f\{e\}$ we have therefore
$f\{a\}=e\cdot f\{a\}-(a\cdot u-u\cdot a)$. It follows that $f$ cobounds
if and only if the $(1,e\cdot\mathfrak{P})$-cocycle $\hat f$, where
$\hat f\{a\}=e\cdot f\{a\}$, cobounds. Thus, in proving that every
1-dimensional cocycle of $\mathfrak{A}$ cobounds, we may confine our attention to those
two-sided $\mathfrak{A}$-modules $\mathfrak{P}$ for which the identity $e$ of $\mathfrak{A}$ is the left
identity operator.

Since $\mathfrak{A}$ is separable there exists a finite algebraic extension $\Gamma$ of
$\Phi$ such that $\mathfrak{A}_\Gamma$ is the direct sum of full matrix algebras over
$\Gamma$; say $\mathfrak{A}_\Gamma=\Gamma_{n_1}+\cdots+\Gamma_{n_m}$. [uses `Hochschild1945.Cited_separable_splitting`] If $f$ is any
$(1,\mathfrak{P})$-cocycle of $\mathfrak{A}$ over $\Phi$ we define a $(1,\mathfrak{P}_\Gamma)$-cocycle
$f^*$ of $\mathfrak{A}_\Gamma$ by setting
$f^*\{\sum_{i=1}^n\gamma_i a_i\}=\sum_{i=1}^n\gamma_i f\{a_i\}$.
Let $e^q_{i,j}$ $(i,j=1,\cdots,n_q)$ denote the matrix units of $\Gamma_{n_q}$.
Then $e^q_{i,j}e^r_{k,p}=\delta_{q,r}\delta_{j,k}e^r_{i,p}$, and
$\sum_{q=1}^m\sum_{i=1}^{n_q}e^q_{i,i}=e$. Consider now the element
$u^*=\sum_{q=1}^m\sum_{i=1}^{n_q}e^q_{i,1}\cdot f^*\{e^q_{1,i}\}$ of
$\mathfrak{P}_\Gamma$: We have
\[
\begin{aligned}
e^r_{h,t}\cdot u^*-u^*\cdot e^r_{h,t}
&=\sum_{q=1}^{m}\sum_{i=1}^{n_q}e^r_{h,t}e^q_{i,1}\cdot f^*\{e^q_{1,i}\}\\
&\quad-\sum_{q=1}^{m}\sum_{i=1}^{n_q}e^q_{i,1}\cdot
 \bigl(f^*\{e^q_{1,i}e^r_{h,t}\}-e^q_{1,i}\cdot f^*\{e^r_{h,t}\}\bigr)\\
&=\sum_{i=1}^{n_r}e^r_{h,t}e^r_{i,1}\cdot f^*\{e^r_{1,i}\}
 -\sum_{i=1}^{n_r}e^r_{i,1}\cdot f^*\{e^r_{1,i}e^r_{h,t}\}
 +e\cdot f^*\{e^r_{h,t}\}\\
&=f^*\{e^r_{h,t}\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
By linearity, it follows that $f^*\{a^*\}=a^*\cdot u^*-u^*\cdot a^*$, for
every $a^*\in\mathfrak{A}_\Gamma$. In particular, $f\{a\}=a\cdot u^*-u^*\cdot a$,
for every $a\in\mathfrak{A}$. The question of whether there exists an element $u\in\mathfrak{P}$
such that $f\{a\}=a\cdot u-u\cdot a$, for every $a\in\mathfrak{A}$ can be reduced
to the question of whether a certain system of linear equations with coefficients
in $\Phi$ possesses a solution in $\Phi$. The last equation means that there
does exist a solution in $\Gamma$. Hence, there must already be a solution in
$\Phi$, and we have proved that every 1-dimensional cocycle of $\mathfrak{A}$ is a coboundary.

Conversely, suppose that $\mathfrak{A}$ is an algebra over $\Phi$ such that
$H^1(\mathfrak{A},\mathfrak{P})=\{0\}$ for every two-sided module $\mathfrak{P}$. It is known that
under these circumstances $\mathfrak{A}$ is semi-simple\textsuperscript{8}. We shall,
however, reproduce the proof here since it will throw some light on the
significance of the 1-dimensional cohomology groups.

As is well known, a necessary and sufficient condition for an algebra to be
semi-simple is that every representation be completely decomposable into
irreducible parts. This in turn is equivalent to the following condition: If
$\mathfrak{P}$ is any left $\mathfrak{A}$-module, $\mathfrak{Q}$ an $\mathfrak{A}$-invariant subspace of $\mathfrak{P}$,
then there exists a (complementary) $\mathfrak{A}$-invariant subspace $\mathfrak{R}$ such that
$\mathfrak{P}$ is the direct sum of $\mathfrak{Q}$ and $\mathfrak{R}$. [uses `Hochschild1945.Cited_semisimple_representations`]

We shall show that this condition is satisfied if all the 1-dimensional
cohomology groups of $\mathfrak{A}$ are $\{0\}$:

Given the left $\mathfrak{A}$-module $\mathfrak{P}$ and an invariant subspace $\mathfrak{Q}$, let us first
choose any linear subspace $\mathfrak{S}$ of $\mathfrak{P}$ such that $\mathfrak{P}$, as a linear
space, is the direct sum of $\mathfrak{Q}$ and $\mathfrak{S}$. For any $s\in\mathfrak{S}$ and $a\in\mathfrak{A}$
we may write $a\cdot s=S_a\{s\}+Q_a\{s\}$, where $S_a\{s\}$ is a uniquely
determined element of $\mathfrak{S}$ and $Q_a\{s\}$ a uniquely determined element of
$\mathfrak{Q}$. Clearly, $S_a$ and $Q_a$ are linear mappings of $\mathfrak{S}$ into $\mathfrak{S}$ and
$\mathfrak{Q}$ respectively. From the relation $a_1\cdot(a_2\cdot s)=a_1a_2\cdot s$
and the fact that the sum $\mathfrak{Q}+\mathfrak{S}$ is direct we obtain the relations
\[
S_{a_1}S_{a_2}=S_{a_1a_2}\quad\hbox{and}\quad
Q_{a_1}S_{a_2}+a_1*Q_{a_2}=Q_{a_1a_2},
\]
where $a*Q$ is defined by $(a*Q)\{s\}=a\cdot Q\{s\}$.

Now, let $\mathfrak{M}$ denote the linear space of all linear mappings of $\mathfrak{S}$ into
$\mathfrak{Q}$. We make $\mathfrak{M}$ a two-sided $\mathfrak{A}$-module by the definitions:
$(a*M)\{s\}=a\cdot M\{s\}$, $M*a=MS_a$, for $M\in\mathfrak{M}$, $a\in\mathfrak{A}$,
$s\in\mathfrak{S}$. It is easy to see from the above relations that the mapping
$a\to Q_a$ is a $(1,\mathfrak{M})$-cocycle of $\mathfrak{A}$. By our hypothesis, there exists
an element $M_0\in\mathfrak{M}$ such that $Q_a=a*M_0-M_0S_a$, i.e.
$Q_a\{s\}=a\cdot M_0\{s\}-M_0\{S_a\{s\}\}$. Now, consider the mapping
$s\to s-M_0\{s\}$ of $\mathfrak{S}$ into $\mathfrak{P}$. This maps $\mathfrak{S}$ onto some
linear subspace $\mathfrak{R}$ of $\mathfrak{P}$. We have
$a\cdot(s-M_0\{s\})=S_a\{s\}+Q_a\{s\}-a\cdot M_0\{s\}
=S_a\{s\}-M_0\{S_a\{s\}\}$, which shows that $\mathfrak{R}$ is $\mathfrak{A}$-invariant.
It is obvious that the mapping $s\to s-M_0\{s\}$ is a linear isomorphism,
whence $\dim(\mathfrak{R})=\dim(\mathfrak{S})$. Furthermore, it is easy to see that
$\mathfrak{R}\cap\mathfrak{Q}=\{0\}$. Hence $\mathfrak{P}$ is the direct sum of $\mathfrak{Q}$ and $\mathfrak{R}$.
This completes the proof that $\mathfrak{A}$ is semi-simple.

Hence, what we have to show now is that if $\mathfrak{A}$ is semi-simple and inseparable
there exist a two-sided $\mathfrak{A}$-module $\mathfrak{P}$ and a non-cobounding
$(1,\mathfrak{P})$-cocycle of $\mathfrak{A}$. Since $\mathfrak{A}$ must have an inseparable simple
component and since any non-cobounding 1-cocycle of a simple component of $\mathfrak{A}$
can be trivially extended to give a non-cobounding 1-cocycle of $\mathfrak{A}$ we may
suppose from now on that $\mathfrak{A}$ is simple. [uses `Hochschild1945.Cited_inseparable_simple_component`] Then—as is well known—the center $\mathfrak{C}$
of $\mathfrak{A}$ is a field which is algebraic and inseparable over $\Phi$. [uses `Hochschild1945.Cited_simple_inseparable_center`] In the case
where $\mathfrak{A}$ itself is an inseparable extension field of $\Phi$, the result in
question follows immediately from the known theory of derivations—i.e.,
$(1,\mathfrak{C})$-cocycles of $\mathfrak{C}$—in fields of characteristic
$p$.\textsuperscript{9} Of the results of this theory we shall require only
the following lemma:

We can now begin the construction of a non-cobounding 1-cocycle of the simple inseparable algebra $\mathfrak{A}$. If $m$ is the dimension of $\mathfrak{A}$ over its center $\mathfrak{C}$ the regular representation of $\mathfrak{A}$ over $\mathfrak{C}$ provides us with an isomorphic mapping $a\to M_a$ of $\mathfrak{A}$ into the matrix algebra $\mathfrak{C}_m$ ($m$-rowed square matrices with elements in $\mathfrak{C}$). It follows that the definitions $a\cdot M=M_aM$, $M\cdot a=MM_a$ make $\mathfrak{C}_m$ (regarded as a linear space over $\Phi$) a two-sided $\mathfrak{A}$-module.

Now let $D$ be a derivation of $\mathfrak{C}$ over $\Phi$ which does not map all of $\mathfrak{C}$ into zero (such a $D$ exists, by Lemma 4.1). [uses `Hochschild1945.Lem_4_1`] If $M=(c_{ij})$ is any element of $\mathfrak{C}_m$ we define $D\{M\}=(D\{c_{ij}\})$ and verify that this is a derivation of $\mathfrak{C}_m$ over $\Phi$. If we now set $f\{a\}=D\{M_a\}$, it is clear that $f$ is a $(1,\mathfrak{C}_m)$-cocycle of $\mathfrak{A}$. If $c\in\mathfrak{C}$, we must obviously have $M_c=cI_m$, where $I_m$ denotes the identity matrix in $\mathfrak{C}_m$. Hence, $f\{c\}=D\{c\}I_m$, which is different from zero for some $c\in\mathfrak{C}$. On the other hand, if $f$ were a coboundary, we should have a matrix $M_0\in\mathfrak{C}_m$ such that $f\{a\}=M_aM_0-M_0M_a$, for every $a\in\mathfrak{A}$. But this would imply that $f\{c\}=0$, for every $c\in\mathfrak{C}$. Hence, $f$ cannot cobound. Thus, we have proved the following theorem:

Consider the $(1,\mathfrak{P})$-cocycle $f'$ of $\mathfrak{A}$ defined by: $f'\{a\}=f\{a\}-a\cdot u+u\cdot a$. Then $f'\{b\}=0$, for every $b\in\mathfrak{B}$, i.e. $\hat f'=0$. Furthermore, $b\cdot f'\{a\}-f'\{ba\}+f'\{b\}\cdot a=0$, since $f'$ is a cocycle. This reduces to $b\cdot f'\{a\}=0$, and similarly, $f'\{a\}\cdot b=0$, for all $b\in\mathfrak{B}$ and all $a\in\mathfrak{A}$. Thus $f'$ maps $\mathfrak{A}$ into $\mathfrak{Q}$. Clearly, $f'$ may be regarded as a $(1,\mathfrak{Q})$-cocycle $f^*$ of $\mathfrak{A}/\mathfrak{B}$. If $f^*$ cobounds there exists an element $v\in\mathfrak{Q}$ such that $f^*\{a\}=a\cdot v-v\cdot a$. But then $f\{a\}=a\cdot(u+v)-(u+v)\cdot a$, i.e. $f$ cobounds. Hence the mapping $f\to f^*$, which is determined to within a coboundary, defines an isomorphism of the kernel of our homomorphism $H^1(\mathfrak{A},\mathfrak{p})\to H^1(\mathfrak{B},\mathfrak{p})$ into $H^1(\mathfrak{A}/\mathfrak{B},\mathfrak{Q})$.

Finally, if $h^*$ is any $(1,\mathfrak{Q})$-cocycle of $\mathfrak{A}/\mathfrak{B}$ we can define a $(1,\mathfrak{P})$-cochain $h$ of $\mathfrak{A}$ by the relation $h\{a\}=h^*\{\bar a\}$, where $\bar a$ is the coset of $a\bmod\mathfrak{B}$. It is easily seen that $h$ is actually a cocycle which vanishes on $\mathfrak{B}$. Obviously, $h$ is mapped into $h^*$ by the above isomorphism, which is therefore an isomorphism \emph{onto} $H^1(\mathfrak{A}/\mathfrak{B},\mathfrak{Q})$. This proves Theorem 5.1.

Then the kernel of the natural homomorphism of $H^1(\mathfrak{A},\mathfrak{P})$ into $H^1(\mathfrak{B},\mathfrak{P})$ is isomorphic with $H^1(\mathfrak{A}/\mathfrak{B},\mathfrak{Q})$, where $\mathfrak{Q}$ is regarded as a two-sided $\mathfrak{A}/\mathfrak{B}$-module.
